blocks.content: The story starts with a choice that every database makes before you write a single line of code.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305492563-371640449.png
blocks.alt: A banking transfer that must be atomic and consistent, compared with an Instagram like counter where a brief delay is acceptable

blocks.content: You're building a banking system. A user transfers ₹10,000 from Account A to Account B. The money must leave A and arrive at B. If the system crashes between those two operations, the money cannot vanish. The database must guarantee that both happen or neither happens. Correctness is non-negotiable.

Now you're building Instagram's like counter. A post gets 50,000 likes per minute. If the like count shows 49,832 instead of 49,847 for a few seconds, nobody cares. If your database can't keep up with 50,000 writes per second and the app slows to a crawl, everybody cares. Availability is non-negotiable.

These two systems need fundamentally different things from their databases. ACID gives you the first. BASE gives you the second. They are not competing standards they are different contracts, built for different problems.
1. ACID
ACID is a set of four guarantees that a database makes about every transaction.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305494421-738135354.png
blocks.alt: ACID transaction guarantees: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability

blocks.content: Together they ensure that even in the presence of crashes, power failures, and concurrent users, your data is always in a valid, consistent state.

["Atomicity: Either all operations succeed together or all fail together; there is no partial completion.
","Consistency: Every transaction keeps the database in a valid state and does not violate any rules or constraints.
","Isolation: Multiple transactions run independently without seeing each other's intermediate changes.
","Durability:  Once a transaction is committed, the data is permanently saved, even if the system crashes.
"]
items: Atomicity: Either all operations succeed together or all fail together; there is no partial completion.
Consistency: Every transaction keeps the database in a valid state and does not violate any rules or constraints.
Isolation: Multiple transactions run independently without seeing each other's intermediate changes.
Durability:  Once a transaction is committed, the data is permanently saved, even if the system crashes.

blocks.content: ACID Properties Explained Using a Bank Transfer
blocks.text: ACID Properties Explained Using a Bank Transfer

blocks.content: Atomicity: You send ₹10,000 from A to B.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305496073-182500816.png
blocks.alt: Atomicity example: debit and credit are one indivisible unit, a crash before the credit rolls back the debit

blocks.content: The transaction does two things: debit A by ₹10,000, credit B by ₹10,000. If the server crashes after the debit but before the credit, the database rolls back the debit on recovery.
You never end up with money debited from A but not credited to B. The transaction is atomic it's one indivisible unit, not two separate operations.
Consistency: Your database has a rule: no account balance can go below zero.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305497592-449909673.png
blocks.alt: Consistency example: a transfer that would violate the no-negative-balance constraint is rejected, keeping the database in a valid state

blocks.content: If Account A has ₹5,000 and someone tries to transfer ₹10,000, the transaction violates the constraint and is rejected.

Consistency means business rules foreign keys, unique constraints, check constraints are always enforced. The database moves from one valid state to another valid state, never through an invalid state.
Isolation: You have ₹10,000. Two transfers of ₹10,000 each are submitted simultaneously.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305499230-188851765.png
blocks.alt: Isolation example: two simultaneous ₹10,000 transfers are serialized so only one succeeds instead of both draining the balance

blocks.content: Without isolation, both could read the balance as ₹10,000, both pass the balance check, both debit ₹10,000, and your balance goes to -₹10,000. Isolation prevents this. The transactions serialise one sees the result of the other and the second one fails because the balance is already zero.
Durability: The database says "committed." The commit acknowledgement reaches your application.
blocks.text: Durability: The database says "committed." The commit acknowledgement reaches your application.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027624-773289935.png
blocks.alt: Durability example: the commit is written to the Write-Ahead Log and synced to disk before acknowledgement, so it survives a crash and restart

blocks.content: The server catches fire. You restart. The committed transaction is there written to the Write-Ahead Log, synced to disk before the commit acknowledgement was sent.
The data is not in memory. It is on disk, permanently.
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

blocks.content: The Cost of ACID
ACID guarantees make databases reliable, but they also add overhead.

The database must maintain transaction logs, check constraints, manage locks or multiple row versions, and ensure data is safely written to disk before confirming success. All of this takes time and resources.

Because of these guarantees, ACID databases prioritize correctness over raw speed. They can handle large workloads, but when systems need extremely high throughput at internet scale, ACID guarantees can become a bottleneck.
In short: ACID provides strong consistency and reliability, but the extra work required to maintain those guarantees comes at the cost of performance and scalability.
Transaction Isolation Levels
Most databases let you trade isolation strength for performance. This is one of the most important things to understand about ACID in practice
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305502510-474114830.png
blocks.alt: Transaction isolation levels from Read Uncommitted to Serializable, with the anomaly each level prevents

blocks.content:
["Read Uncommitted: Can read uncommitted data from other transactions. Dirty reads are possible.
","Read Committed: Only reads committed data. Dirty reads are prevented.
","Repeatable Read: Reading the same row multiple times gives the same result during the transaction.
","Serializable: The strongest isolation level. Transactions behave as if they run one by one.
"]
items: Read Uncommitted: Can read uncommitted data from other transactions. Dirty reads are possible.
Read Committed: Only reads committed data. Dirty reads are prevented.
Repeatable Read: Reading the same row multiple times gives the same result during the transaction.
Serializable: The strongest isolation level. Transactions behave as if they run one by one.

blocks.content: More Isolation = More Consistency = Lower Performance

Most applications use Read Committed or Repeatable Read. Serializable is chosen when correctness is absolutely critical financial ledgers, inventory management, medical records. The lower isolation levels exist because Serializable has real performance costs it requires range locks or predicate locking that dramatically reduces concurrency.
2. BASE
BASE emerged from the engineering reality of building systems at web scale.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305503988-728434085.png
blocks.alt: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft State, and Eventually Consistent

blocks.content: Databases like Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, and Riak made availability and partition tolerance their primary goals. They gave up strict consistency. BASE describes the resulting contract.
BASE stands for: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually Consistent.

["Basically Available: The system always returns a response, even if the data is stale or incomplete.
","Soft State: The system's data can change over time as replicas synchronize with each other.
","Eventually Consistent: If no new updates occur, all replicas will eventually have the same data."]
items: Basically Available: The system always returns a response, even if the data is stale or incomplete.
Soft State: The system's data can change over time as replicas synchronize with each other.
Eventually Consistent: If no new updates occur, all replicas will eventually have the same data.

blocks.content: BASE prioritizes Availability over immediate Consistency.
BASE Properties Explained Using a Instagram
blocks.text: BASE Properties Explained Using a Instagram

blocks.content:
["Basically Available: When you open Instagram, you always get a response. Some posts, likes, or comments may be slightly outdated, but the app remains available instead of showing an error.
","Soft State: After you like a post, some servers may show the updated like count while others may not. The system is temporarily in different states as data is being synchronized.
","Eventually Consistent: After a short time, all servers receive the update and show the same like count. The data eventually becomes consistent everywhere.
"]
items: Basically Available: When you open Instagram, you always get a response. Some posts, likes, or comments may be slightly outdated, but the app remains available instead of showing an error.
Soft State: After you like a post, some servers may show the updated like count while others may not. The system is temporarily in different states as data is being synchronized.
Eventually Consistent: After a short time, all servers receive the update and show the same like count. The data eventually becomes consistent everywhere.

blocks.content: 3. How Eventual Consistency Works

When a user performs an action, the write is saved on one server first. That server then asynchronously propagates the update to other replicas. Because replicas update in the background, there is a short period where different servers may have different data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305505589-236743688.png
blocks.alt: A write is acknowledged immediately by the primary node, then asynchronously replicated to other replicas with a brief window of inconsistency

blocks.content: Imagine you like a post on Instagram.
The request first reaches the Primary Node. The Primary Node immediately saves the change and sends a success response (ACK) back to you. From your perspective, the operation is completed instantly.
At this moment, only the Primary Node has the latest data. The other replicas still have the old data.

After sending the response, the Primary Node starts asynchronous replication in the background. It sends the update to Replica 1, Replica 2, and Replica 3. Since this happens asynchronously, the replicas do not update at exactly the same time.

During this short period, different servers may have different data. For example, if another user reads from Replica 2 before it receives the update, they may still see the old like count. This temporary inconsistency is normal.
A few milliseconds or seconds later, all replicas receive the update from the Primary Node and store the same data. Once every replica has been updated, the system becomes eventually consistent.
4. The CAP theorem: Why this trade-off exists
blocks.text: 4. The CAP theorem: Why this trade-off exists

blocks.content: ACID and BASE sit at opposite ends of a fundamental trade-off described by the CAP theorem. A distributed system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously:
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027807-663952885.png
blocks.alt: The CAP theorem: a distributed system can only guarantee two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance, and partition tolerance is not optional

blocks.content: Network partitions are not optional. In any distributed system, packets get dropped, networks split, data centres lose connectivity.
Partition Tolerance is a requirement, not a choice. So the real trade-off is always: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice Consistency or Availability?

["CP systems (ACID): when a partition occurs, some nodes refuse to serve requests rather than risk returning stale data. The system goes partially unavailable but stays consistent. PostgreSQL with synchronous replication: if a replica can't be reached, the primary stops accepting writes rather than risk data loss.
","AP systems (BASE): when a partition occurs, nodes keep serving requests from whatever data they have. The system stays available but returns potentially stale data. Cassandra: all nodes accept writes even if they can't reach each other. Conflicts are resolved after the partition heals.
"]
items: CP systems (ACID): when a partition occurs, some nodes refuse to serve requests rather than risk returning stale data. The system goes partially unavailable but stays consistent. PostgreSQL with synchronous replication: if a replica can't be reached, the primary stops accepting writes rather than risk data loss.

AP systems (BASE): when a partition occurs, nodes keep serving requests from whatever data they have. The system stays available but returns potentially stale data. Cassandra: all nodes accept writes even if they can't reach each other. Conflicts are resolved after the partition heals.

blocks.content: 5. ACID vs BASE
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305508755-225363774.png
blocks.alt: ACID (strong consistency, locked transactions, sacrifices availability) compared side by side with BASE (high availability, no locks, sacrifices immediate consistency)

blocks.content: 6. ACID vs BASE Databases (Which databases give you which)
blocks.text: 6. ACID vs BASE Databases (Which databases give you which)

blocks.content: Databases such as PostgreSQL, MySQL (InnoDB), Oracle, SQL Server, CockroachDB, and Google Spanner are generally considered ACID databases. They prioritize strong consistency, reliability, and transactional correctness.

Databases such as Cassandra, DynamoDB, Redis Cluster, Riak, CouchDB, and MongoDB (for most operations) are commonly associated with BASE principles. They prioritize availability, scalability, and eventual consistency.

However, modern databases are no longer strictly ACID or BASE. Many databases allow developers to choose the level of consistency they need. For example, Cassandra supports QUORUM reads and writes, where a majority of replicas must agree before a response is returned.
DynamoDB provides strongly consistent reads as an option when stronger consistency is required. MongoDB also supports multi-document ACID transactions.

The key takeaway is that the line between ACID and BASE is becoming increasingly blurred. Modern databases often combine features from both approaches, allowing developers to balance consistency, availability, and performance based on the application's requirements.
7. When to Choose ACID vs BASE
blocks.text: 7. When to Choose ACID vs BASE

blocks.content: 1. Choose ACID when correctness is more important than performance.

["For financial transactions, money must never disappear or be duplicated. If ₹10,000 is transferred from one account to another, both the debit and credit must happen correctly.
","For inventory management, if only one item is left in stock, two customers should not be able to purchase it at the same time.
","For medical records, doctors must always see accurate and consistent patient information. Partial or outdated data can lead to incorrect treatment.
","For authentication and authorization, a user either has permission or does not. Inconsistent permissions can create security risks.
"]
items: For financial transactions, money must never disappear or be duplicated. If ₹10,000 is transferred from one account to another, both the debit and credit must happen correctly.
For inventory management, if only one item is left in stock, two customers should not be able to purchase it at the same time.
For medical records, doctors must always see accurate and consistent patient information. Partial or outdated data can lead to incorrect treatment.
For authentication and authorization, a user either has permission or does not. Inconsistent permissions can create security risks.

blocks.content: 2. Choose BASE when availability and scalability are more important than immediate consistency.

["For social media feeds, seeing a post or like count a few seconds late is acceptable, but the application should always remain available.
","For like counts and view counts, slight temporary differences are not important because the values will eventually become correct.
","For product catalogues, showing a slightly outdated description or price for a few seconds is usually acceptable.
","For activity logs and analytics, high write throughput is more important than immediate consistency.
","For user preferences, such as dark mode or language settings, a small delay in synchronization across devices is generally not a problem.
"]
items: For social media feeds, seeing a post or like count a few seconds late is acceptable, but the application should always remain available.
For like counts and view counts, slight temporary differences are not important because the values will eventually become correct.
For product catalogues, showing a slightly outdated description or price for a few seconds is usually acceptable.
For activity logs and analytics, high write throughput is more important than immediate consistency.
For user preferences, such as dark mode or language settings, a small delay in synchronization across devices is generally not a problem.

blocks.content: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">8. The mixed architecture ( Using both in one system )
blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">8. The mixed architecture ( Using both in one system )

blocks.content: Most production systems at scale use ACID and BASE for different parts of the same application. The key insight is that different data in the same system has different consistency requirements.
ACID

ACID databases are used for data where correctness is non-negotiable. If the data becomes inconsistent, it can lead to financial loss, security issues, or business failures. This is why systems use ACID for orders, payments, inventory, and user authentication.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305510307-394540431.png
blocks.alt: ACID databases are used for orders, payments, inventory, and user authentication where correctness is non-negotiable

blocks.content: For example, when a customer places an order, the order record must be created correctly. When a payment is processed, money must be debited and credited accurately.
If only one item is left in stock, ACID ensures that two customers cannot purchase it simultaneously. Similarly, user roles and permissions must always be consistent to prevent unauthorized access.
Because ACID provides strong consistency, transactions, and isolation, it is the preferred choice for critical business data.
Examples: Orders, Payments, Inventory, Banking, Medical Records, User Accounts, Authentication.
BASE

BASE databases are used for data where high availability and scalability are more important than immediate consistency. A small delay in data synchronization is acceptable because the data will eventually become consistent.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305511878-429356121.png
blocks.alt: BASE databases are used for social media feeds, product catalogues, search indexes, recommendation systems, and session caches

blocks.content: For example, when you open Instagram or Twitter, seeing a post or like count that is a few seconds old is usually not a problem. Product catalogues can show slightly outdated information temporarily.

Search indexes may take a few seconds to reflect newly added content. Recommendation systems and caches also work well with eventual consistency because absolute accuracy is not required at every moment.
BASE systems sacrifice immediate consistency to achieve better performance, availability, and scalability.
Examples: Social Media Feeds, Product Catalogues, Search Indexes, Recommendation Systems, Analytics, Activity Logs, Session Caches.
9. Hard Consistency Problems

1. Read Your Own Writes: A user creates a post or comment and immediately refreshes the page. The new content is missing because the read request went to a replica that has not received the latest update yet.
Solution: Route reads to the primary for a short time after a write, use session stickiness, or use synchronous replication.
2. Monotonic Reads: A user sees a post with 100 likes. After refreshing, the same post shows 95 likes because the second request hit a replica that is further behind.
Solution: Keep the user on the same replica (session pinning) or use read quorums.
3. Write Conflicts (Multi-Master Systems): Two users update the same record on different nodes at the same time. Both updates are accepted, creating a conflict during replication.
Solution: Use Last Write Wins (LWW), CRDTs, or application-level conflict resolution.
10. HLD interview ( How to talk about this )
blocks.text: 10. HLD interview ( How to talk about this )

blocks.content: When a design question involves data storage, consistency is always worth discussing explicitly. The strongest answers show you can reason about which consistency model is right for each part of the system.

Frame the trade-off clearly. "ACID gives us correctness every read sees the latest committed write, transactions are atomic, constraints are always enforced. We pay for this with throughput limitations and the risk of blocking during failures. BASE gives us availability and throughput we can serve millions of requests per second, we never block, but reads may be slightly stale. The right choice depends on what 'wrong' looks like for each piece of data."

Apply it to the specific system. For a ride-sharing app: "The payment transaction charge rider, pay driver must be ACID. A double charge or a missing payment is a catastrophic bug. I'd use PostgreSQL. The ride history feed and driver location updates can be BASE DynamoDB for ride history at scale, with Redis for the real-time location cache. Slightly stale location data on the map is fine. An incorrect charge is not."

Show you know the spectrum. "Most modern databases offer tunable consistency Cassandra's QUORUM reads give you near-ACID behaviour for reads that need it, while ONE reads give you maximum throughput for reads that don't. I'd use that knob intentionally rather than applying one setting globally."

Address eventual consistency's user-visible problems. "One thing I'd design carefully is read-your-own-writes. After a user creates a post, they should immediately see it in their feed even if we're using eventual consistency. I'd solve this by routing the feed read to the primary for 2–3 seconds after a write, or by including the just-created post in the UI optimistically before the replica catches up."

The engineers who give the best answers are the ones who treat ACID and BASE not as tribal preferences "we always use Postgres" or "we always use Cassandra" but as tools with specific trade-offs that you choose deliberately based on the consistency requirements of each piece of data.
